lines.text: I wish someone told me this before I started coding. You can undo almost anything in Git.
Most beginners panic, delete the whole folder, and start again. You don't have to.
Here are the five oh-no moments, and the exact command that fixes each one.
Oh-no number one. You commit, then notice you forgot a file, or your message has a typo.
Just add the file, and run git commit, dash dash amend. It replaces your last commit with a fixed one.
Want to unpack the commit completely? Git reset, dash dash soft, head tilde one. Tilde one means one commit back.
The commit disappears, but every change stays, ready to commit again.
Oh-no number two. You ran git add on a file that shouldn't go in yet.
Git restore, dash dash staged, and the file name. It comes out of the staging area, and your edits stay safe.
Oh-no number three. You've broken a file, and you just want the last saved version back.
Git restore, and the file name. Your changes are thrown away, and the file goes back to your last commit.
Careful with this one. Those changes were never committed, so they're gone for good. Not sure? Run git stash instead, and bring them back later.
But what if the mistake is already on GitHub, and your team has pulled it?
Quick thing. Git, GitHub and GitHub Actions is a free course. You can learn it on Teyro.
Okay. Back to the mistake.
Oh-no number four. The bad commit is already on GitHub.
Don't reset it. Your teammates already have that commit. Rewrite it, and their history no longer matches yours.
Use git revert, and the commit's ID. Revert doesn't delete anything. It adds a new commit that does the exact opposite. Safe for everyone.
Oh-no number five. You deleted a branch, with a week of work on it.
Here's the secret most beginners never learn. Git keeps a diary. It's called the reflog.
Every time your HEAD moves, Git writes it down. Run git reflog, find your lost commit, and make a new branch right there.
Even commits you overwrote with amend are in there. By default, lost commits stay in the diary for thirty days.
And here's the rule behind all of this. Anything you committed can almost always be recovered. Anything you never committed is likely gone forever.
So commit early. Commit often.
So. Committed too early? Amend. Wrong file staged? Restore staged. Broken file? Restore. Already pushed? Revert. Lost a branch? Reflog.
Git doesn't punish mistakes. It just needs you to commit.
